You can use Amazon Comprehend to build smart applications, such as an application that

Amazon Comprehend uses pre-trained models to analyze documents and gather insights – the
model is continuously trained on a large body of text. In addition, you can customize the
service to your specific requirements by building custom NLP models using your proprietary
data. Here, you can define custom classification and custom entity recognition.
Although AWS offers a wide range of AI and ML tools pretrained with massive datasets,
sometimes you need to build custom models with your training data. Amazon SageMaker AI
enables you to design and build your own models and is discussed next.
Building your own models with Amazon SageMaker
AI
Businesses may often need to build their own machine learning models based on their
industry and idx_120eb270 specific requirements. To that end, Amazon offers its machine learning solution
called Amazon SageMaker AI. Previously known as just Amazon SageMaker, this service
enables your data scientists and developers to quickly build, train, and deploy ML models into
a production-ready hosted environment. You do not need to procure and manage expensive
hardware, allowing you to focus on building and developing your ML workflows.
You build your machine learning models to generate predictions or insights by training them
with an algorithm and sample data. Once the model has been trained, you embed it into your
application so it can produce real-time, scalable inferences. The workflow is depicted in Figure
14.3:

Chapter 14 424
Summary
In this chapter, you learned about several Machine Learning tools and AI services. AWS offers a
vast array of fully managed machine learning tools that you can use to build complex AI- and
ML-driven applications for your business requirements.
As part of your exam preparation, ensure that you are fully aware of core machine learning
tools such as the ones discussed in this chapter. Each machine learning service is designed to
offer specific functions, such as Amazon Polly, which converts text to speech, and Amazon
Transcribe, which can transcribe audio files into text.
Amazon ML tools such as Amazon Rekognition, Polly and others are fully managed, so you do
not need to procure or manage your own infrastructure. Even if you need to build your own
training models for custom use cases, AWS offers the SageMaker suite of tools and services
enabling you to focus on your business goals and objectives.
So far you have manually designed and deployed various infrastructure services such as S3
buckets, EC2 instances, and RDS databases using the AWS management console. However,
businesses do not want to spend time building, configuring, and managing underlying
infrastructure. Furthermore, using the AWS management console to manually create resources
using mouse clicks and keyboard entries often leads to inconsistencies in how components are
configured.
The next chapter introduces you to tools to automate the design, build, and deployment of
infrastructure using PaaS tools and Infrastructure as Code (IaC). These services enable you to
build infrastructure resources in a manner that is consistent, repeatable, and predictable.

Automation, Management
and Governance, and
Security on AWS
Building applications and provisioning infrastructure using Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and
Platform as a Service (PaaS) solutions helps ensure architectures and resources are deployed
in a repeatable and consistent manner. Whether you deploy a set of resources once or multiple
times, you can be confident that the architecture is provisioned with the correct configuration
and follows the intended design every time. Services such as CloudFormation and Elastic
Beanstalk are designed specifically for this purpose. In addition, following DevOps practices
and implementing a Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline
enables you to deliver application updates and enhancements more efficiently and reliably.
This part also covers the core management and governance services required to manage,
monitor, and support workloads, applications, and infrastructure resources deployed on AWS.
Finally, security must be considered from the outset of any cloud solution. You will learn about
key security best practices, including encryption and network auditing, and explore a range of
tools and services available to help protect your applications and infrastructure from malicious
attacks.
This part of the book includes the following chapters:

Automation, Deployment, and
Additional AWS Services
Businesses use cloud services to either offload their on-premises workloads, build hybrid cloud
solutions, or develop cloud-native applications. Companies do not want to really concern
themselves with provisioning and managing core underlying infrastructure if possible – their
primary concern is the ability to host scalable, highly available, secure, and cost-effective
applications for their internal business needs or customer-facing requirements.
To that end, businesses want to be able to deploy their applications that consume less
administrative burden and ensure smooth ongoing releases and updates. Businesses must
focus on what matters most to them – not the underlying heavy lifting of infrastructure
services and resources.
In Chapter 10, you deployed a complete marketing campaign website for Belly Brew Co.
Limited. However, you had to manually provision all the underlying infrastructure resources
such as VPCs, EC2 instances, load balancers, auto scaling groups, and databases. What if you
could automate the deployment of these resources using a Platform as a Service (PaaS) tool?
Services like Amazon Elastic Beanstalk allow you to upload your application code, select the
appropriate language and framework, and provision all the necessary resources for you, rather
than you having to manually use the console to deploy the required resources.
Another approach is to provision your resources using code – specifically, Infrastructure as
Code (IaC) solutions that require you to use a declarative language script to build out the
configurations of your resources. AWS provisions these resources exactly as you define them in
your code. This approach ensures repeatable deployments, making it easier to deploy the
architecture across multiple accounts and environments with a single click. You get
consistency in your deployment configurations, the ability to version your build solutions, and
faster provisioning.
In this chapter, you will learn about these automation provisioning tools and the PaaS
solution. You will also be introduced to the basic concepts of DevOps and how organizations
manage their application releases and updates using Continuous Integration and
Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) tools.
The following topics are covered in this chapter:
Deploying applications using AWS Elastic Beanstalk
Architecting and deploying infrastructure using AWS CloudFormation
Introducing CI/CD with AWS Developer tools
Introducing Amazon Q
Deploying applications using AWS Elastic Beanstalk
AWS Elastic Beanstalk is a idx_90635d31 PaaS offering that enables you to upload and deploy your
application without having to manually configure any underlying resources. AWS provisions

even databases, based on your specified requirements for the application stack. This means
you do not need to spend hours managing infrastructure resources, and your developers get to

The service also offers management and logging capabilities, includes capacity provisioning
and health monitoring, and ensures high availability and scalability. You simply upload your

Chapter 15 432
With AWS Elastic Beanstalk, you idx_d9103f23 have the same range of flexibility in how you configure and
deploy your resources as any manual deployment—you can choose your EC2 instance type,
decide on auto scaling policies, and define how your load balancers should be configured.
These features allow you to retain control but without the complexity of manual
configurations.
Next, you will learn more about some of the core components of AWS Elastic Beanstalk.
Core components of AWS Elastic Beanstalk
When working with idx_065ace85 AWS Elastic Beanstalk, you idx_4a6e03c5 create an application. Think of this as a folder
in Elastic Beanstalk that groups related environments and versions of the same app. It is within
the application container that you manage all the Elastic Beanstalk objects related to your
application.
An application can have multiple versions, enabling you to test the differences between them.
It is a pointer to a ZIP/WAR file in an Amazon S3 bucket that contains the application code.
Before you deploy your application, you idx_6f1abcd4 must create an environment, which is a collection of
AWS resources that will run the application, such as EC2 instances, load balancers, runtimes,
and language frameworks. Each environment can only run one application version at a time;
however, you can run multiple environments simultaneously. This is how you can host
different stages of your application, such as:
Development: used by developers to build new features or fix bugs
Testing: used for alpha and beta testing
Production: the live environment accessed by end users
When you create an environment, you must idx_934bdbee define the environment tier. The environment
tier describes how traffic reaches your application and tells AWS what resources to provision.
There are two tiers:
Web Server environment: used for idx_a96b209c applications' HTTP and HTTPS requests (for
example, websites and API calls)
Worker environment: used for idx_c348b00c background processing applications that receive jobs
from a queue
Figure 15.1 depicts the two Elastic Beanstalk environment tiers for a typical application that
comprises a frontend and backend workload.
•
•
•
•
•
433 Automation, Deployment, and Additional AWS Services
Figure 15.1: AWS Elastic Beanstalk environments
The following are the idx_16377df2 key components of the architecture as depicted in Figure 15.1:
The application is served by an Application Load Balancer that accepts requests using
standard HTTP and HTTPS protocols. This is typical of a website or web application
delivery.
The Web Server Tier comprises the EC2 instances, which host the frontend user
interface (UI) of the application and may be supported by an auto-scaling group that is
managed by the Elastic Beanstalk service. Incoming requests to the Application Load

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 432
chunks.content:
Balancer are evenly distributed to the available EC2 instances across the availability
zones.
The Worker Tier is designed to process background application logic. It is supported by
an auto-scaling group to scale as required based on the number of requests held in the
SQS queue, which is designed to decouple the application stack. The Elastic Beanstalk
service will install a daemon on each EC2 instance in the fleet. The daemon is used to
read messages from the SQS queue and send this data to the application servers
running in the worker environment for processing.
The Amazon SQS queue is used to store messages as requests from the front-end web
server tier, which the resources in the worker tier will pull based on capacity and
availability. This ensures a decoupled architecture and reduces overburdening the
backend idx_ca8c53f6 application services.

Chapter 15 434
In this section, you learned about the AWS Elastic Beanstalk service, which is a PaaS solution.
The service is designed to handle the infrastructure heavy lifting, provisioning, managing, and
maintaining all the required underlying resources so that developers can focus on their
application code and business logic.
In the next section, you will learn about another automation tool designed to help you
architect and deploy infrastructure resources idx_64b49072 using Infrastructure as Code (IaC) – specifically,
AWS CloudFormation.
Architecting and deploying infrastructure using AWS
CloudFormation
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is a idx_43936472 process by which you define and describe your infrastructure
resources and their configurations in a scripted template written using a data serialization
language such as YAML or JSON.
Data-serialization languages are used to convert structured data into a format that can be
stored, transmitted, and read by another system, without losing its meaning.
AWS CloudFormation uses idx_70392fc4 data-serialization languages like YAML and JSON to read the
structured description of your AWS resources, build a dependency graph, and then provision
the infrastructure automatically. This is also known as declarative scripting.
This is different from imperative scripting using languages like Python or Java, which require
you to explicitly describe the step-by-step instructions on how to carry out those
configurations.

The next section provides further details on how these templates are defined.
CloudFormation templates
AWS CloudFormation uses idx_ad809235 templates, which are text files written in JSON or YAML. The script
describes the resources to provision, along with mandatory and optional configuration options
required to provision the resources.
For example, if you need to deploy an EC2 instance in the default VPC, in a default subnet, and
attach it to the default security group, you can provide a CloudFormation template such as the
YAML code below:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Description: >
Basic CloudFormation template to launch a single EC2 instance in the default

chunks.content:
VPC and default subnet.

MyEC2Instance:
Type: AWS::EC2::Instance
Properties:
# Use an Amazon Linux 2023 AMI us-east-1 Region (update AMI ID per region!)
ImageId: ami-07ff62358b87c7116
InstanceType: t2.micro # Define Instance Type
# By not specifying a SubnetId, EC2 will launch in the default subnet
# By not specifying the Security Group, EC2 will launch with the default
Security Group

- Key: Name
Value: MyFirstCFNInstance
Some key points to note in the code:
The AWS template idx_f4786321 format version is set to "2010 ‑ 09 ‑ 09" and is the current and only
supported version.
A Description field is used to explain the purpose of the template.
There are various sections of the templates, such as Parameters, Mappings, Resources,
Outputs, and others.
The Resources section is the only mandatory section. This section is used to describe
what AWS resources will be created. In this case, it's the AWS::EC2::Instance resource.

An AMI ID must be specified when launching an EC2 instance. AMIs are region-specific,
so you must provide an AMI ID that exists in the region where the resources are being
provisioned. You can use the Mappings section to define AMIs based on the region the
template is being deployed in, making the template more dynamic.
Some properties such as InstanceType, SubnetId, and SecurityGroupIds may need to
be defined depending on your requirements. If SubnetId and SecurityGroupIds are
idx_5794d50a not specified, AWS automatically uses the default subnet and default security
group of the default VPC.
Once the template is defined, it is uploaded to AWS CloudFormation to create a stack, which
provisions the actual AWS resources. CloudFormation passes the properties to the EC2 service.
When SubnetId or SecurityGroupIds is missing, EC2 automatically applies the default VPC,
default subnet, and default security group.
In the next section, you will learn more about CloudFormation stacks.
CloudFormation stacks
When you create and upload a idx_62bddac1 CloudFormation template, you deploy what is known as a
Stack. A stack idx_60d7a078 is a collection of one or more AWS resources that are deployed and managed as a
single unit using CloudFormation. For example, using a single template, you can provision a
VPC, load balancers, auto-scaling groups to provision EC2 instances, and even a backend
Amazon RDS database, all part of that single stack.
How you build out your stack deployment is also critical. For example, you can use more
advanced techniques to modularize the various infrastructure elements of your environment
as separate templates. You can then use either:
Cross-Stack References: Where you build a base stack, such as a VPC, and allow other
stacks to reference idx_b362ab93 values from it (for example, Subnet IDs or Security Groups) so that
compute or database resources can be deployed into the same underlying environment
without being part of the same stack.
Nested Stacks: Where you modularize each infrastructure element, such as VPCs, EC2
instances, and RDS instances, as separate templates and invoke them from a main
parent template idx_52f4ac16 to build a complete end-to-end infrastructure for an application. This
allows you to organize infrastructure into logical components while still managing
everything through a single parent stack, making updates and ongoing management
easier
When you need to delete idx_46448d67 the resources deployed by CloudFormation, you simply delete the
stack. AWS will then terminate all the resources it created following your template. This

ensures orphan resources are not left lingering, which often happens when you manually
delete several infrastructure resources.

Sometimes you may need to update or modify a stack. For example, when you need to upgrade
an EC2 instance type from a t3.micro to a t3.large. In the next section, you will learn more
about how you can achieve this using AWS CloudFormation Change Sets.
AWS CloudFormation change sets
If you need to change the idx_0a59ce4c configuration of your cloud resources to cope with changing
requirements or demand, you need a way to upgrade or modify existing resources without
having to rebuild the entire stack. This is particularly true if the change you need to make
should not affect the application.
AWS CloudFormation offers a idx_167af945 feature known as Change Sets, which is where you upload a
modified version of your template or even supply a new template as a change to the existing
stack configuration. AWS CloudFormation will then provide a visual representation of your
proposed changes and notify you if the change will require resource replacements.
In Figure 15.2, you will note that a change set has been requested to upgrade the EC2 instance
type from a t3.micro to a t3.small.
Figure 15.2: Change Set request to upgrade the EC2 instance type from t3.micro to t3.small
Once you have reviewed the proposed change, you can then execute the change set, and AWS
will perform the modifications as required.
Change sets are particularly useful in highlighting how the change proposed will impact the
existing architecture and if any resources will be affected. You can then take any necessary
precautions, such as performing backups and taking manual snapshots before executing the
change.
AWS CloudFormation makes it easy to build infrastructure solutions in a consistent, repeatable
manner with predictable outcomes. You can build a wide range of templates to quickly deploy

your resources using idx_ef590fcf CloudFormation rather than manually configuring each resource using
the web console, which often leads to inconsistencies and errors.
In addition to automating your infrastructure provisioning and deployment using tools like
Elastic Beanstalk and CloudFormation, you must also consider your application lifecycle that
runs on the provisioned infrastructure. Modern architectures recommend applying DevOps
principles and best practices when designing how your applications are deployed, updated,
and released into production environments. The next section introduces you to this concept
and the tools offered by AWS to build an effective DevOps pipeline.
Introducing CI/CD with AWS developer tools
Managing the application lifecycle is crucial to ensure that users always have access to the
latest and most reliable version of an application, without bugs or performance issues. This
means development teams must continuously enhance the application, introduce new
features based on customer feedback, and resolve issues in a timely manner. In addition,
releasing the application into production must follow a carefully planned strategy, ensuring
that new features and bug fixes are deployed with minimal disruption and that rollbacks are
simple if something goes wrong.
DevOps idx_f3fe68ae is a set of practices that brings development (Dev) and operations (Ops) teams
together to collaborate across the entire application lifecycle. Rather than delivering large
releases every few months or once a year, DevOps promotes small, frequent, and incremental
releases aligned with the principles of CI/CD (Continuous Integration and Continuous
Delivery/Deployment). Instead of working in silos, DevOps encourages automation and
continuous feedback, allowing applications to be released faster, more reliably, and with fewer
errors.
AWS provides a wide range of tools and services to build, test, deploy, and operate
applications, while improving quality, stability, and customer satisfaction.
In the following subsections, we will look at a high-level overview of some of these tools.
AWS CodeCommit
Developers write and maintain code for their applications, which must be continuously
updated, revised, and versioned as new features are added and bugs are fixed. AWS
CodeCommit is a idx_991b448f fully managed, secure source control service that hosts Git-based
repositories, enabling teams to manage source code versions and track changes efficiently.
CodeCommit can be used to store application source code, configuration files, scripts, and
documentation. It works with standard Git tools and commands, making it easy for developers
439 Automation, Deployment, and Additional AWS Services
who already use Git on other platforms to adopt CodeCommit without changing their existing

chunks.heading: Chapter 15 438

workflows.
AWS CodeBuild
AWS CodeBuild is a fully managed idx_fb5388ba build service. Developers use CodeBuild to compile source
code, run unit tests, and build artifacts that can then be deployed on AWS. There is no need to
provision your own build servers, and the service offers prepackaged build environments for
popular languages and build tools. All you need to do is provide a buildspec file, which is a
collection of build commands and related settings, in YAML format. AWS CodeBuild uses this
file to run a build.
Finally, you are charged on a pay-as-you-go model, making the offering very cost-effective
rather than hosting your own build servers.
AWS CodeDeploy
Once an application has been idx_1d0ab8c4 built and compiled, AWS CodeDeploy can be used to automate
the deployment of the application to Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon Elastic Container
Service (ECS), AWS idx_f717dda0 Lambda functions, and on-premises servers. CodeDeploy helps ensure
that application updates are delivered in a consistent and repeatable way.
CodeDeploy deploys application revisions and supporting artifacts that are typically stored in
services such as Amazon S3 or external repositories like GitHub and BitBucket. The service
enables rapid and reliable application releases, including updating Lambda function versions,
while helping to avoid application downtime during deployments. This is achieved using
different deployment strategies, such as in-place deployments, where instances are updated
gradually (for example, by taking a defined number of instances offline at a time), and blue/
green deployments, where the existing application version (blue environment) continues to
run while a new version is deployed to a separate environment (green environment). Once
testing and approvals are complete, traffic can be shifted to the new version.
One of the key benefits of idx_91fbf227 AWS CodeDeploy is its centralized control over application
deployments, including the ability to monitor deployment status, stop deployments, and roll
back automatically if errors occur.
AWS CodePipeline
AWS CodePipeline is a fully managed idx_860db6f5 continuous delivery solution you can use to automate
your application releases and updates. CodePipeline integrates with the previously mentioned
tools (CodeCommit, CodeBuild, and CodeDeploy) to automate the build, test, and deployment
of your application releases every time your code changes, as depicted in the following
workflow in Figure 15.3:

chunks.content:

Figure 15.3: AWS CodePipeline orchestration
The following steps explain the workflow of the AWS CodePipeline service:
The developer pushes the source code to the AWS CodeCommit repository
A commit to CodeCommit triggers an AWS CodePipeline workflow
The Source stage of CodePipeline pulls the latest code from the CodeCommit repository
The Build stage uses AWS CodeBuild to compile, test, and package the application
The Deploy stage uses AWS CodeDeploy to deploy the application
AWS idx_93e921d8 CodeDeploy then deploys the application to the target EC2 instance
CodePipeline doesn't store code, build applications, or deploy workloads; it simply
orchestrates the entire CI/CD workflow.
In the next section, you will learn how developers can use AI tools on AWS to help them write
code and design application workflows using a product called Amazon Q.
Introducing Amazon Q
Amazon Q is a idx_f298acd5 fully managed generative AI service that acts as an intelligent assistant for
working with AWS. Using natural language processing (NLP), you can ask questions about
AWS architectures, best idx_d18398f6 practices, troubleshooting, cost, and the state of your own resources —
all in plain English.
Amazon Q is powered by Amazon Bedrock, a fully managed service that provides access to a
wide range of foundation models (FMs) through idx_b8eb65eb standard API calls. This is what allows

Amazon Q to understand your questions and respond with context-aware, AWS-specific
guidance.
In practical terms, Amazon Q supports you throughout the application lifecycle. For example,
you can describe a requirement — such as building a secure web application or creating an
Amazon ECS Fargate environment — and Amazon Q can suggest suitable AWS services aligned
with best practices, recommend architectural patterns, and explain unfamiliar configurations.
Directly inside the AWS Management Console, you can also ask Amazon Q about your existing
resources and costs and have it return the answers as tables and charts. This enables even non-
developers to move from idea to working solution faster while staying aligned with AWS Well-
Architected design principles.
